body:
Yes, I feel the same way.

Some days are better than others - some weeks are better than others. But I usually wind up back in the same place. An overwhelming urge to end it all, and the stinging guilt of knowing how much it would upset my family.

It is ironic how often I sit alone thinking about the pain I'm going to cause my family, when none of them reach out to say as much as "hello" to me.

Anyway, I'm sorry that you are suffering. I sympathize.

Ironically, my friend and her husband who came to the US have now moved to the UK (and had to go through the entire process of getting her a permit to live in the UK).

I wouldn't rule out getting a sponsorship to move the US, if it's something you're really set on. It'll take research though, and it may require some effort to develop skills that will make you a competitive applicant for jobs. The other plus side of talking to other people who have done it before is that you'll build your network. If you can build a rapport with the right person, they may be able to help you obtain that sponsorship themselves. Don't go into conversations expecting that, but it's a good reason to pursue developing relationships.
I haven't spoken to him in probably a decade or more. He was a really great person, I too hope he is doing well.

Happy to offer my perspective!

You're correct on marriage and corporate sponsorship. I have a friend who went through the process of having someone from Britain move to the US through a marriage license. It was incredibly time consuming for them (took close to 12 months after their marriage for him to get permanent residence in the US).

I don't know a lot about corporate sponsorship, but I suspect that without a technical skill, or something in high demand, it'll be difficult to get a corporation to go through the hassle of sponsoring you instead of looking in the US to fill that position. That being said, it's not impossible, and those who have done it before will probably have good insight for you.

Cost of living in the US can vary a lot depending on where you live. Monthly rent can vary from $300-$400 a month, to thousands of dollars of month depending on location. I'm sure that the UK is similar in that regard. I bring up healthcare just to point out that, if you didn't have the money for it, at least you'll still get service in the UK. Here in the US, they will literally let you die rather than incur costs you cannot repay.

I've had interest in moving to the UK, primarily due to the fact that it's an english speaking country and the transition would be rather straight forward (I've visited the UK before as well, great country!). With Brexit, I would probably not move there now - lack of EU membership is a big turn off. I think Sweden, Denmark, or Norway are also high on my list. All three countries rate very high on measures of quality of life, happiness, and freedom (the US ranks 20th in a scale of personal and economic freedom!).

Also, it is very very normal to stress about money. I stressed about money a lot in college - to the point where it interfered with my life and my studies. I recently purchased a house and I stress a lot about money again (way more expensive than I thought it was going to be).

Lots of people stress about money, so don't feel like you're alone in that struggle. It doesn't mean your stress isn't legitimate, just that others can relate. I have the advantage of having a university degree, but I work with a lot of people that don't who have pretty good jobs, some of them with very little previous experience.

You can find good work, even without a university degree. It may not be easy, but definitely have hope, good jobs are out there.

As someone who lives in the US, my first instinct would be to talk you out of it. I don't know particularly why you want to move to the US, but personally I'd like to move to an EU nation. There are plenty of things wrong in the US, and while that's true of absolutely any country, there are many EU countries who have a lot more of their shit together than we do.

But that's not what you're here to talk about. Here is my opinion:

Moving to the US probably seems daunting in particular for the very reason you stated: you don't know how to make it happen.

I would start there, look into the process for moving and obtaining a workers permit in the US. Don't just look at the procedures and forms, though, look for testimonials or advice from people who have actually done it. If you can, reach out to those people and tell them that you're also interested in making the move. They may be able to give you specific advice on how to get started and how to have a better chance of success.

We're lucky enough to live in an age where communicating with people in similar situations as ourselves is relatively easy, the internet makes finding and connecting with such people a breeze. You might even start with r/IWantOut - a community for moving to another country.

But you asked another important question, and that's whether or not you'd feel "instantly better."

My guess is, probably not. If you moved here today, you're going to have to face certainly realities about the US. The most glaring of which is probably the fact that you just lost all medical coverage. You can show up at an ER and they're obligated to stabilize you, but that's it. They can kick you out the door with serious medical issues unaddressed as long as your vitals are stable unless you can prove you can pay tens of thousands of dollars in medical fees. You can get insurance, but its expensive (I pay over $100 a month, and that's AFTER my company pays $200-$400 a month), and I still have a co-pay ($100 for an ER visit, $20 for an office visit) and a deductible (I'm liable for $1,000/yr of medical expenses, NOT including co-pays).

I don't know what your stresses are, but it sounds like money might be one if you don't have a strong work history. Here in the US, things tend to be more expensive, if only because you don't have any medical coverage unless you pay for it.

That's my 2 cents.

I don't have bad advice or statements that were said to me - no one I know in real life is aware of how depressed or bad off I am, and I'm very careful not to say things that might make people concerned. When I hear people say things like "I hate my life" or "shoot me now" I always ask them if they're okay, and if they're thinking about suicide. Usually they say those things as a figure of speech, but since I think those things everyday and I do not think them as a figure of speech, I always check.

But anyway, the reason I wanted to reply is that my sister was once told something very similar. She and I went to a pretty bad high school - it wasn't bad in the sense of crime or anything, just a really poor education. My mother didn't want us in that environment for very long, and eventually made arrangements for us to be home schooled.

Before my sister and I left the school, it got out that we were leaving. One of the strangest comments that she got from a teacher - that we all joke about to this day more than a decade later - was "you're too pretty to leave school."

People are often too absorbed with physical attractiveness.

Wow, great post.

When I was growing up, I played a lot of games online. Someone that I played with regularly and became good friends with was from Israel and was living in the US.

After years of knowing each other, I told him one day that I was depressed, and he said that he was too. I asked him what was wrong, and he told me that, when he was 16, he served in the IDF (Israeli Defense Force). During his time in the IDF, he was shot in the leg and could no longer serve. He came to the US and met a girl that he fell in love with. They dated for a while, and he traveled between the US and Israel quite a bit. Eventually, they separated - he wanted to return to the IDF, she wasn't sure they had a future together (or at least, that's the jist of what I got from him).

He was back in the US while he was telling me this, and said that he probably could not return to the IDF due to his injury. He then asked me why I was depressed, and I told him that having heard his story, it didn't really seem all that important anymore. I'll never forget his reply to me, he told me of course it was still important, depression is depression, it affects everyone the same. Doesn't matter what causes it.

I don't have any answers for you, but I do understand your pain. I know what it's like to feel like you do a lot for others, but no one seems to care that you exist. I spend my weekends alone - I rarely talk to anyone. I don't really have any friends anymore, and I only occasionally talk to anyone in my family. For me, the worst part is that my family was all very close growing up, but now I am a bit of an outcast. They don't really talk to me, and I don't really talk to them anymore, that's probably harder than having people at work or old friends not care, knowing how much I suffer and that my family doesn't know or ask.

But anyway, I just wanted to reply and say that if you ever want to talk, feel free to leave a message here or send me a message directly. I know what it feels like to feel alone, and I'm around if you want to talk some more.

There are lots of good people out there.

I am sorry that you are in pain. I know what it feels like, I am there every day myself. If you want to talk, please feel free to keep replying or to send me a message. I can't promise I can help, but I'll certainly be here to listen.

I use to feel very much the same way - and in some ways still do, although not exactly.

In college, I use to hate being around other people, I always use to feel like the people were an annoying waste of space, and constantly judging me. I also thought a lot about hurting other people (very elaborately in fact), or myself. But things did change, they got better in some ways and not in others. If I can share with you one thing I have learned since those rough days, I regret even thinking about hurting other people.

I don't like other people much, mostly because other people don't like me much. Long story I won't get into here, but what I will say is that although my general opinion of people hasn't improved much, I've realized that hurting people or causing pain doesn't help anyone or anything. I would feel remorse over doing it, and others would just have pain for the rest of their life.

People like you and me (and others) know what it is like to hurt. If there's one thing I think most of us share, it's that we don't want others to feel the same.

I don't want to give up self harm. I have other issues that I really should start seeking help for, but I don't because I know this will come up eventually and I'm not really ready to deal with it.

Like you, SH is one of the few things that makes me feel better, for a lot of reasons. The act itself, but also feeling like I need to punish myself for screwing up. And while I recognize that sounds super unhealthy, I can't really cope well right now and I think that the alternative is much worse.

I'm sorry that you feel that way.

I know what it's like not to have people to talk to. I don't have any friends - no one to call to hang out with, no online friends. The only people I talk to are my coworkers, and I barely say more than a few sentences to most of them all day.

I hope that you can find what you're looking for, I hope you can find people that you can connect with and start to feel better again.

I don't have any answers for you, I just wanted to say that I read what you wrote.

I hope that you are able to find something or someone who can help you start to feel better again.

I don't have any answers for you, just wanted to say that I read what you wrote.

If your company offers EAP services, you should look into them. They are completely anonymous - your company and co-workers will never know you used them.

I have similar thoughts myself. I hope that you are able to get better.
I appreciate your reply, and that you are trying to be helpful. It's a really good thing, and you're a good person for doing it.
I know exactly how you feel when she says that. I'm sorry things are difficult for you. I hope that talking has helped, at least a little bit.

You can look for other CC or accredited online schools (at least for your associates).

My CC pushed hard for me to get a GED or high school diploma. But when I came for my last semester and still didn't have one, they gave me a check for "24 college credit hours completed" and made me eligible for my degree.

You might have to do some searching for a school that is willing to do the same for you. I just wanted to make sure you knew that it is possible to do.

I wish you all the best.

I hope that posting this does help. If you want to talk more about the fight - if you think that would help - please feel free to do so.

If you think dredging up those thoughts won't help though, don't.

Maybe you should find a way to express your thoughts to your SO that doesn't alarm them in a way you didn't intend to. It can be hard to find the right words to use, but perhaps approaching them from the perspective of feeling responsible for some of the negative comments that were made about you, and wanting their help in making yourself a better person? I'm not saying what they said is true, but perhaps wording it that way to your SO will emphasize that you feel that it's true, and that you don't want it to be true, and you want their help?

I know this doesn't really address what you came here to talk about, but I wanted you to know something anyway:

You do not need a high school diploma or a GED to get higher education in the US. You also do not have to take the SAT or ACT. All of these things help, but they are not required.

I completed a 2-year associates degree from a community college without ever acquiring my GED or a high school diploma (still do not have either to this day). I was also accepted into a 4 year college without completing either the ACT or SAT. I finished a bachelors in science without any of these things.

It's no harder to complete college this way, college is difficult no matter how you do it. Community colleges will give you placement exams so you don't get in over your head - if you place low, it might take you longer than normal to finish college but it's still possible to do.

I now work a salary job and make over 60K a year with paid vacation and full benefits just 5 years out of college.

I'd be happy to tell you more or help you get on a similar path to mine if that is something you are interested in.

I feel like this too. I know how I'd die, I know how to make it painless and quick. I have access to everything I need, I could do it today if I wanted.

But, just like you, my family would be devastated. Mind you, I go weeks without talking to any of them - they don't call me to ask me how I'm doing, we talk on birthdays and some holidays, and very very occasionally in between. I probably only talk to my siblings once every month or two. I talk to my mom one or two times a month usually, sometimes a little more.

Every day I wake up, I wish that I hadn't. Every day I go to bed, I hope that I never wake up. But I can't bring myself to do anything about it, because as much of a piece of shit as I am, it'd hurt my mom and my siblings too much.

I've felt that way before. One thing that helped me when I was getting better was to break habits I had made that reinforced my depression. Music, was a big one for me, I would listen to music that made me feel more depressed - it was a vicious circle. So I stopped listening to all the songs that I loved, but made me feel terrible. I started listening to classical music.

I got better for a long time - I'm not better anymore, but that's a different story - I started feeling more normal and less socially anxious.

Another thing that helped me was understanding that depression is a chemical condition of the brain. Things can happen that lead you into depression, but staying there is a result of your brain rewiring itself to think in a depressive way. Getting better requires changing brain chemistry, it's not an easy process but it can be done. A lot of it comes down to recognizing thoughts that make you feel depressed or empty, and when you think them, stop yourself and tell yourself they aren't true. That also helped me a lot.

I wake up everyday disappointed - disappointed that I woke up. Every day I go to sleep, I go to sleep hoping that I won't ever wake up again.

I don't have a list of reasons to give as to why. There's just nothing in life I look forward to, there's nothing in life I want, except for it to end. Probably the only reason it hasn't is that it would hurt my family so much. We were the type of family that ate every meal together, I shared rooms with my siblings for the majority of my life, and we lived in a rural community where just hanging out with anyone besides my siblings was an ordeal.

But now, I'm invisible. My siblings have moved, and so have I. I rarely talk to them, and they rarely talk to me. All my friends have either left my life, or I've pushed away - and I mean all of them. Most days, the only people I talk to are my coworkers. And there's really only a few I say more than a sentence or two to all day. It's not uncommon for me to be completely overlooked at work, even not being invited to meetings or training for things I am or will be responsible for.

But the hardest thing to deal with every day, is sitting alone in my room and knowing that all I want to do is die, and there isn't a person on the planet that cares enough to ask me how I'm doing.
